alerts: Support and moments do not usually identify a unique distribution.
A marginal distribution does not define dependence.

topics.title: Bounds, thresholds, atoms, mixtures and tails

questions.text: What does one value of the quantity measure?
questions.help: The answer sets the support: the set of values that the law can give.

options.label: A count: 0, 1, 2, …
One result with two values: yes or no
One category from a fixed list
Counts in several categories, with a fixed total
A rank, such as the rank of a word by frequency
A waiting time or a lifetime
A proportion or a probability, from 0 to 1
Shares of a whole: proportions with the sum 1
A positive size or amount, such as a loss or a file size
The largest or the smallest value of each period or block
A measurement that can be negative, such as an error or a change
Several measurements together, which can have a correlation

questions.text: Which mechanism makes the count?
questions.help: A mechanism that you know gives the strongest reason for a law.

options.label: Successes in a fixed number n of independent trials, each with the same probability
Successes in n draws without replacement from a finite population
Independent events at a constant rate, in a fixed time, length or area
Failures before a success: the first success or success number r
Events at a rate that changes between units or periods
The total of a random number of groups, each with a random size
A value from a to b, each value with the same probability

questions.text: Which success ends the count?
questions.help: The count is the number of failures before this success.

options.label: The first success
Success number r, with r larger than 1

questions.text: Which mechanism makes the time?
questions.help: The hazard rate is the rate of the event at time t, given no event before t.

options.label: The chance of the event in the next short time does not depend on the time already waited
The time is the sum of k stages, each with the same constant hazard rate
The hazard rate changes with age: wear or early failures
The time is the product of many independent positive factors
The first time that a random process gets to a level

questions.text: How does the hazard rate change with age?
questions.help: Use failure records or knowledge of the wear mechanism.

options.label: It increases as a power of the age
It increases exponentially with the age, as human mortality does
It decreases: early failures
It increases, then decreases

questions.text: Does the process move toward the level on average?
questions.help: This is the drift of the process.

options.label: Yes: the process has a positive drift toward the level
No: the process has no drift

questions.text: Which mechanism makes the size?
questions.help: A size is a positive amount, such as a loss, a claim or a file size.

options.label: The product of many independent positive factors
The sum of many independent positive parts
The total of a random number of individual amounts
A power law: the number of values above x decreases as x^(−α)
The excess of a value over a high threshold
The total of many independent amounts with an infinite variance

questions.text: Where does the power law start?
questions.help: The power law describes the right tail. The body of the law can have a different shape.

options.label: At a minimum value x_m larger than 0: no value is below x_m
At 0: small values are possible, and the density decreases from 0
After a mode: small values are rare, and large values follow the power law

questions.text: What is the proportion?
questions.help: A proportion takes values in [0, 1].

options.label: A probability or a fraction that changes between units or is not known exactly
A value between known limits, with no other information

questions.text: Which extreme value is it?
questions.help: A block is a period or a batch, such as one year of daily values.

options.label: The maximum of many values in each block
The minimum of many positive values: the weakest part
Each value above a high threshold

questions.text: Which mechanism makes the measurement?
questions.help: Each mechanism here has a theorem or a definition that gives a law.

options.label: The sum of many small independent effects with a finite variance
Usually small, but sometimes very large deviations
The difference of two independent exponential times
The difference of two independent Gumbel values, such as a latent value in a logistic model
The ratio of two independent normal values with mean 0
The sum of many independent values with an infinite variance
A sum of squares of independent standard normal values
A ratio of two independent variance estimates
A mean divided by its estimated standard error
A value between known limits, each value equally likely

questions.text: Does the count have a known upper limit?
questions.help: An example is the number of machines that fail in a group of n machines.

options.label: Yes: the count cannot be more than a known number n
No: there is no fixed upper limit

questions.text: How does the variance of the count compare with its mean?
questions.help: Use data or knowledge of the mechanism. This is the dispersion of the count.

options.label: About equal
The variance is larger: overdispersion
The variance is smaller: underdispersion

questions.text: Are there more zeros than a Poisson or a negative binomial law gives?
questions.help: An example is a count of claims, with many policies that can never have a claim.

options.label: Yes: there are too many zeros
No

questions.text: How fast does the probability of a very large value decrease?
questions.help: This is the right tail of the law. A finite sample cannot identify the tail.

options.label: There is a finite upper limit
At least as fast as an exponential function: a light tail
Slower than all exponential functions, but all moments exist
As a power x^(−α): a heavy tail, and some moments do not exist

questions.text: Do some exact values occur with a positive probability?
questions.help: An example is a loss that is exactly 0 for most policies. Such a value is an atom of the law.

options.label: Yes: many values are exactly 0
Yes: other exact values
No

questions.text: Is the population a mix of groups that behave differently?
questions.help: An example is a histogram with two peaks.

options.label: Yes
No

questions.text: How are the values recorded?
questions.help: The observation mechanism decides the law of the recorded values.

options.label: Each value is recorded exactly
A value beyond a limit is recorded only as “beyond the limit”
A value beyond a limit is not recorded
The chance to record a value depends on the value

questions.text: Are the values independent of each other?
questions.help: A law of one value does not say how the values depend on each other.

options.label: Yes: they are independent
No: values close in time are related
No: each event makes more events likely soon after
No: each value makes the next values, as parents make offspring
No: several variables depend on each other or on a common cause

questions.text: How does the process change over time?
questions.help: A stationary process keeps the same law at all times.

options.label: It keeps the same behaviour: it is stationary
It moves between a finite number of states
It drifts or grows
It has sudden jumps at random times, a few in each period
It moves by jumps of all sizes, also many small jumps

questions.text: Do extreme values of the variables occur together?
questions.help: Tail dependence is the limit of the probability that one variable is extreme, given that another variable is extreme, as the level becomes more extreme.

options.label: Large values occur together
Small values occur together
Large values and small values occur together
No: extreme values do not occur together more than the correlation gives

questions.text: How many variables depend on each other?
questions.help: Some copulas give the same dependence to every pair of variables.

options.label: Two
More than two, with different dependence for each pair

questions.text: Which data do you have?
questions.help: The rejection tests need data. Without data, each candidate is a hypothesis.

options.label: No data: only knowledge of the mechanism
Fewer than about 30 values
About 30 values or more
Several thousand values, enough to use them directly

questions.text: On what does the decision depend?
questions.help: A decision on a tail needs more evidence about the tail than a decision on a mean.

options.label: A mean value, such as an expected cost
A tail probability or a high quantile, such as a capacity or a reserve
The largest value in a period
The whole distribution

evidence.label: Mean value
evidence.help: From data or from knowledge. For a yes-or-no result, the probability of yes.

evidence.label: Standard deviation
evidence.help: Larger than 0. A negative binomial law needs a variance larger than the mean.

evidence.label: Upper limit or number of trials n
Threshold of the decision
evidence.help: The record estimates P(X > c), or P(X ≤ c) for a rank.

examples.label: Pump seal faults at a constant rate
Ticket holders who come to the flight
Claims for each policy, with a rate that changes between policies
Failed attempts before the first good connection
A positive loss with an unknown tail, for a reserve

candidates.name: Bernoulli

competing.text: The probability depends on other variables. Then a conditional model gives each unit its own probability.
Several results of the same kind are counted together. Their sum is binomial when the results are independent.

tests: Independence: a runs test on the sequence of results.
Same probability for all units: compare the fractions of yes in groups with a chi-square test.

candidates.name: Binomial

competing.text: When n is large and p is small, Poisson(np) is close. The total variation distance is at most np².
The draws are without replacement from a small population. Then the trials are not independent.
The probability p changes between groups. Then the variance is larger than np(1 − p).

tests: Dispersion: the sample variance must be near np̂(1 − p̂). A much larger variance rejects a constant p.
Upper limit: no count is larger than n.
Goodness of fit: a chi-square test of the counts against Binomial(n, p̂), with cells pooled to an expected count of at least 5.

requires.text: The mean m must be at most n.

candidates.name: Categorical

competing.text: With many observations, the frequencies of the labels give the probabilities directly.
The probabilities depend on other variables, such as the time of day.

tests: Goodness of fit: a chi-square test of the label counts against the stated probabilities.
Stability: compare the frequencies of the labels in two halves of the data.

extra: probabilities of the labels 1, 2 and 3: illustrative values

candidates.name: Multinomial

competing.text: The probabilities change between groups. Then the counts vary more than the multinomial law permits.
Only the shares matter, not the counts. Then a Dirichlet law can model the shares.

tests: Goodness of fit: a chi-square test of the category counts, with k − 1 degrees of freedom.
Overdispersion: compare the variance of each count between groups with n p_i (1 − p_i).

extra: probabilities of the categories 1, 2 and 3: illustrative values
quantities: prob exceed = X[1] > c "category 1 above the threshold"
mean first = X[1] "mean count of category 1"

candidates.name: Discrete uniform

competing.text: Some values are more likely than others. A categorical law states each probability.
The value is a count of independent successes, so the middle values are more likely.

tests: Goodness of fit: a chi-square test of the counts against equal probabilities.
Limits: no value is below a or above b.

requires.expr: round(2*m) == 2*m and 2*m - lim >= 0 and 2*m - lim <= lim
requires.text: The mean m must be a whole or half number with 0 ≤ 2m − n ≤ n.

candidates.name: Geometric

competing.text: The count ends at success number r, with r larger than 1.
The success probability changes between units. Then the tail is heavier than geometric.

tests: No memory: P(X ≥ k + j | X ≥ k) must equal P(X ≥ j). Compare the ratios in the data.
Dispersion: the variance must be near m(1 + m), with m the mean.
Goodness of fit: a chi-square test against Geometric(1/(1 + m̂)).

requires.text: The mean m must be at least 0.

candidates.name: Negative binomial

competing.text: The rate is the same for all units. Then the variance equals the mean.
Events occur in clusters of random size. A compound Poisson count also has a variance larger than its mean.
The rate takes a few distinct values, such as two types of units.

tests: Dispersion: the variance must be larger than the mean. A variance near the mean supports the Poisson law.
Goodness of fit: a chi-square test against NB(r̂, p̂), with the maximum likelihood estimates.
Clusters: when events occur in groups, test a compound Poisson law.

requires.text: The variance sd² must be larger than the mean m.

candidates.name: Poisson

competing.text: The rate changes between units or periods. Then the variance is larger than the mean.
Each count has a known upper limit n.
Events occur in clusters. Then the count of single items is compound Poisson.

tests: Dispersion: under the Poisson law, (n − 1)s²/x̄ has approximately the χ²(n − 1) law. A value far in either tail rejects the Poisson law.
Goodness of fit: a chi-square test of the counts against Poisson(x̄), with cells pooled to an expected count of at least 5.
Constant rate: compare the mean counts of early and late periods.

candidates.name: Hypergeometric

competing.text: The sample is a small part of the population, or the draws are with replacement.

tests: Limits: the count is at most min(n, K) and at least max(0, n − N + K).
Dispersion: the variance must be near n(K/N)(1 − K/N)(N − n)/(N − 1), smaller than the binomial variance.

extra: population size N: an illustrative value
success items in the population, from the mean

requires.text: The mean m must be at most n.

candidates.name: Zipf

competing.text: With enough data, the rank frequencies of the data need no law.
A lognormal law of the frequencies can also give a rank–frequency plot close to a straight line.

tests: Rank–frequency plot: log frequency against log rank must be close to a straight line with the slope −s.
Goodness of fit: compare a Zipf fit with a lognormal fit by the likelihood ratio (Vuong test).

quantities: prob top = X <= c "a rank of c or better"

candidates.name: Continuous uniform

competing.text: Values near the middle or near one limit are more likely.
The quantity has a law of its own, and the limits only cut it.

tests: Goodness of fit: a Kolmogorov–Smirnov test against the uniform law on [a, b].
Limits: no value is outside [a, b].

requires.text: The standard deviation must be larger than 0.

candidates.name: Normal

competing.text: Large deviations are more frequent than a normal law permits.
The quantity is positive and has a long right tail.

tests: Normal Q–Q plot: the points must be close to a straight line.
Shapiro–Wilk test of normality.
Tails: count the values more than 3 standard deviations from the mean. Expect about 0.27 %.

candidates.name: Multivariate normal

competing.text: Extreme values of the variables occur together. A Student-t copula has tail dependence.
One variable depends on the others in a way that is not linear.

tests: Each marginal law: a normal Q–Q plot.
Mardia's tests of multivariate skewness and kurtosis.
Tail dependence: count the joint exceedances of high quantiles.

extra: correlation of the two measurements: an illustrative value
quantities: prob both = X[1] > c and X[2] > c "both measurements above the threshold c"

candidates.name: Exponential

competing.text: The hazard rate changes with age.
The time is a sum of several stages.
A mix of units with different constant rates. Then the hazard rate decreases.

tests: No memory: the excesses over a threshold must have the same mean as the whole sample.
A plot of log survival against time must be close to a straight line.
Coefficient of variation: it must be near 1.

requires.text: The mean m must be larger than 0.

candidates.name: Gamma

competing.text: The right tail is heavier, and log X looks normal.
The hazard rate is a power of the age.

tests: Gamma Q–Q plot with the fitted shape.
Compare a gamma fit with a lognormal fit and a Weibull fit by the likelihood.

requires.text: The mean m must be larger than 0.

candidates.name: Erlang

competing.text: The number of stages is not an integer, or the stages have different rates.
There is only one stage.

tests: Coefficient of variation: it must be near 1/√k.
Gamma Q–Q plot with the shape k.

extra: number of stages, from the mean and the standard deviation

requires.text: The mean m must be larger than 0.

candidates.name: Beta

competing.text: Only the limits are known.
The values form two or more groups, such as many values near 0 and near 1.

tests: Beta Q–Q plot with the fitted parameters.
Atoms: exact values 0 or 1 do not fit a beta law.

extra: a + b, from the mean and the variance

requires.text: The mean m must be between 0 and 1.
The variance sd² must be smaller than m(1 − m).

candidates.name: Dirichlet

competing.text: The data are counts, not shares.
The shares form distinct groups.

tests: Each share: a beta Q–Q plot, because each marginal law of a Dirichlet law is beta.
Signs of the correlations: in a Dirichlet law, each pair of shares has a negative correlation. A positive correlation rejects it.

extra: concentration of the shares: an illustrative value
quantities: prob big = X[1] > 0.5 "share 1 above one half"

candidates.name: Chi-square

competing.text: The statistic is a ratio of two variance estimates.
The degrees of freedom are not known. A gamma law has a free shape.

tests: The mean must be near k and the variance near 2k.
Conditions of the theorem: independent normal parts with the variance 1.

requires.text: The mean m, the degrees of freedom, must be larger than 0.

candidates.name: Student's t

competing.text: The degrees of freedom are large. Then the t law is close to normal.
Large deviations are frequent, but the tails are exponential.
The variance is infinite, and sums keep the same shape.

tests: Q–Q plot against the fitted t law. Points far from the line in the tails reject it.
Tail index: a Hill plot. The t law with ν degrees of freedom has the tail index ν.

extra: degrees of freedom: an illustrative value

candidates.name: F

competing.text: The denominator has many degrees of freedom. Then d₁F is close to χ²(d₁).
The ratio is of two positive amounts that are not sums of squares.

tests: Conditions of the theorem: independent normal samples in the numerator and the denominator.
The mean must be near d₂/(d₂ − 2), for d₂ larger than 2.

extra: numerator degrees of freedom: an illustrative value
denominator degrees of freedom: an illustrative value

candidates.name: Logistic

competing.text: The tails are lighter. The logistic and normal laws are close in the centre.
The density has a sharp peak at the centre.

tests: Q–Q plot against the fitted logistic law.
Kurtosis: the excess kurtosis must be near 1.2.

candidates.name: Laplace

competing.text: The density is smooth at the centre.
The tails are heavier than exponential.

tests: Q–Q plot against the fitted Laplace law.
Kurtosis: the excess kurtosis must be near 3.

candidates.name: Lognormal

competing.text: The right tail is lighter: exponential, not lognormal.
The right tail is a power law. On a log–log plot of survival, a straight line supports a power law.
The hazard rate is monotone.

tests: Normal Q–Q plot of log X: the points must be close to a straight line.
Tail: a log–log plot of survival must bend down. A straight line supports a power law.

extra: variance of log X, from the mean and the standard deviation

requires.text: The mean m must be larger than 0.

candidates.name: Weibull

competing.text: The hazard rate tends to a constant.
The hazard rate increases, then decreases.
The hazard rate increases exponentially.

tests: Weibull plot: log(−log S(t)) against log t must be close to a straight line with the slope k.
Compare the Weibull fit with an exponential fit by the likelihood ratio: the exponential law is the case k = 1.

requires.text: The mean m must be larger than 0.

candidates.name: Inverse Gaussian

competing.text: The time is a product of factors, not a first passage time.
The process has no drift. Then the first passage time has an infinite mean.

tests: Check the drift: a process with no drift gives the Lévy law instead.
Q–Q plot against the fitted inverse Gaussian law.

requires.text: The mean m must be larger than 0.

candidates.name: Gompertz

competing.text: The hazard rate is a power of the age, not an exponential function.
The population is a mix of groups with different hazard rates.

tests: Log hazard against age must be close to a straight line.
Compare a Gompertz fit with a Weibull fit by the likelihood.

extra: initial hazard divided by b: an illustrative value
rate of growth of the hazard: an illustrative value

candidates.name: Log-logistic

competing.text: The hazard rate also increases, then decreases, but the tail is not a power law.
The tail needs its own shape parameter.

tests: log(S/(1 − S)) against log t must be close to a straight line.
Tail: a log–log plot of survival must become a straight line.

requires.text: The mean m must be larger than 0.

candidates.name: Pareto I

competing.text: Values near 0 are possible.
The log–log plot of survival bends down.
Only the values above a high threshold follow the power law.

tests: A log–log plot of survival must be a straight line from x_m.
Tail index: a Hill plot must be stable over a range of thresholds.

extra: tail index, from the mean and the standard deviation

requires.text: The mean m must be larger than 0.

candidates.name: Pareto II (Lomax)

competing.text: No value is below a known minimum x_m.
The log–log plot of survival bends down.

tests: A log–log plot of survival must become a straight line for large x.
Mean excess plot: it must increase as a straight line.

extra: tail index, from the mean and the standard deviation

requires.text: The mean m must be larger than 0.
A Pareto II law with a finite variance needs sd larger than m.

candidates.name: Burr XII

competing.text: The case k = 1 of the Burr XII law.
The case c = 1 of the Burr XII law.

tests: Compare the Burr XII fit with its special cases, the log-logistic and the Pareto II laws, by the likelihood ratio.
Tail: the tail index ck from the fit must agree with a Hill estimate.

requires.text: The mean m must be larger than 0.

candidates.name: Fréchet

competing.text: The tail type is not known. The GEV law estimates it.
The tail of the values is light.

tests: GEV fit: the shape ξ must be larger than 0.
Return level plot against log return period: it must bend up.

requires.text: The mean m must be larger than 0.

candidates.name: Cauchy

competing.text: The tails are heavy, but the mean exists. The Cauchy law is the t law with 1 degree of freedom.
The tail index is between 1 and 2.

tests: The sample mean does not settle as n increases. The median does.
Q–Q plot against the fitted Cauchy law.

candidates.name: Lévy

competing.text: The process has a positive drift. Then the first passage time has finite moments.

tests: Tail: P(T > t) must decrease as t^(−1/2).
Drift: estimate the drift of the process from its path.

candidates.name: Stable (S0)

competing.text: The variance is finite, and the tails are power laws.
The variance of each part is finite. Then the sum is approximately normal.

tests: Tail index: a Hill plot must give α below 2.
Sums: the law of sums of blocks must keep the same shape after scaling by n^(1/α).

extra: index of stability: an illustrative value

candidates.name: Generalised extreme value (GEV)

competing.text: All values above a threshold are available, not only the block maxima.
The shape ξ is 0.

tests: Probability and quantile plots of the fitted GEV law.
Return level plot with confidence intervals.
Likelihood ratio test of ξ = 0 (the Gumbel law).

extra: shape: an illustrative value; 0 is the Gumbel type
scale, from the standard deviation, exact for ξ = 0

candidates.name: Generalised Pareto (GPD)

competing.text: Only the block maxima are available.
The shape ξ is 0.

tests: Mean excess plot: it must be close to a straight line above the threshold.
Threshold stability: the shape estimate must be stable above the threshold.

extra: shape, from the mean and the standard deviation

requires.text: The mean excess m must be larger than 0.
A generalised Pareto law with these moments needs sd at least m/√11.

candidates.name: Gumbel

competing.text: The shape ξ is not 0.
The values have a power-law tail.

tests: Gumbel plot: −log(−log F) against the sorted values must be close to a straight line.
Likelihood ratio test against the GEV law.

candidates.name: Reverse Weibull

competing.text: The upper limit is not known. The GEV law estimates the shape.
There is no finite upper limit.

tests: GEV fit: the shape ξ must be below 0.
The fitted upper limit must be above the largest observation.

candidates.name: Finite mixture

competing.text: For counts: the rate changes continuously, not between a few groups.
The groups are not known. A kernel density estimate needs no groups.

tests: Compare fits with 1, 2 and 3 components by an information criterion. The likelihood ratio test needs a bootstrap here.
Each component must have a meaning, such as a type of unit.

extra: weights of the two groups: illustrative values
weights of the two groups: illustrative values
weights of the two groups: illustrative values
weights of the two groups: illustrative values
weights of the two groups: illustrative values

candidates.name: Compound Poisson

competing.text: There is no atom at 0, and the total is a sum of a fixed number of parts.
For counts with logarithmic group sizes, the compound Poisson law is negative binomial.

tests: Atom at 0: the fraction of zeros must be near e^(−λ).
Check the number of events and the event sizes apart, when both are recorded.

extra: mean number of events: an illustrative value

requires.text: The mean m must be larger than 0.

candidates.name: Empirical law of the data

competing.text: The quantity is continuous, and values between the observations are possible.
The decision needs values beyond the largest observation.

tests: Size: the decision must not depend on values beyond the largest observation.
Stability: compare the empirical laws of two halves of the data.

quantities: prob top = X <= c "a rank of c or better"

extra: observed values: illustrative, replace them with the data

candidates.name: Kernel density model

competing.text: Only the observed values are possible.
The decision depends on the tail. The tail of a kernel model follows the kernel, not the data.

tests: Bandwidth: the result must not change much when the bandwidth changes.
Tail: the decision must not depend on values far beyond the data.

extra: observed values: illustrative, replace them with the data

candidates.name: Truncated law

competing.text: Values beyond the limit are recorded as “beyond the limit”, not left out.
Only the limits are known.

tests: No recorded value is beyond the limit.
Fit the law with the truncated likelihood f(x)/F(limit). An ordinary fit is biased.

requires.text: The mean m must be larger than 0.
The mean m must be larger than 0.

candidates.name: Censored observation

competing.text: Values beyond the limit are not recorded at all.

tests: Fit with the censored likelihood: the density for the exact values, the survival function for the censored values.
Kaplan–Meier estimate: compare it with the survival function of the fitted law.
candidates.methods: Draw the value from the law, then record min(X, limit) and a flag that says whether X is beyond the limit.

candidates.name: Conditional model

competing.text: The dependence is symmetric, and no variable is a cause of another.

tests: Residuals: given the other variables, the residuals must have the stated law.
Check each conditional law in groups of the other variables.
candidates.methods: Draw the variables in the order of the dependency graph, each from its law given the earlier variables.

candidates.name: Gaussian copula

competing.text: Extreme values occur together.
There are only two variables.

tests: Joint exceedances of high quantiles: they must be rare, because a Gaussian copula with correlation below 1 has no tail dependence.
Goodness of fit of the copula: a Cramér–von Mises test on the ranks.
candidates.methods: Draw a multivariate normal vector, then apply the normal CDF to each part, then the quantile function of each marginal law.

candidates.name: Student-t copula

competing.text: Extreme values do not occur together.

tests: Joint exceedances in the upper tail and in the lower tail: both must be more frequent than under a Gaussian copula.
Compare the t copula with the Gaussian copula by the likelihood.
candidates.methods: Draw a multivariate t vector, then apply the t CDF to each part, then the quantile function of each marginal law.

candidates.name: Clayton copula

competing.text: Large values occur together, not small values.

tests: Joint exceedances below low quantiles must be frequent, and above high quantiles rare.
candidates.methods: Marshall–Olkin method: a gamma frailty value, then independent exponential values.

candidates.name: Gumbel copula

competing.text: Small values occur together, not large values.

tests: Joint exceedances above high quantiles must be frequent, and below low quantiles rare.
candidates.methods: Marshall–Olkin method: a positive stable frailty value, then independent exponential values.

candidates.name: Frank copula

competing.text: There are more than two variables, with different dependence for each pair.

tests: Joint exceedances of high and low quantiles must be rare: the Frank copula has no tail dependence.
Kendall's τ from the data must agree with the τ of the fitted parameter.
candidates.methods: Conditional inverse transform: draw U, then V from the conditional law of V given U.

candidates.name: Finite Markov chain

competing.text: The state is a continuous value, not one of a few states.

tests: Markov property: the next state must not depend on earlier states, given the current state. Compare chains of order 1 and 2.
Stationarity: compare the transition counts of early and late periods.
candidates.methods: Draw each next state from the row of the transition matrix for the current state.

candidates.name: Brownian motion with drift

competing.text: The quantity is positive and grows by percentages.
The path has jumps.

tests: Increments: they must be independent and normal, with a variance proportional to the time step.
Jumps: the largest increments must not be too large for a normal law.
candidates.methods: Exact simulation at the grid times: add independent normal increments.

candidates.name: Geometric Brownian motion

competing.text: The quantity can be negative, and changes add instead of multiply.

tests: Log increments: they must be independent and normal.
Volatility: the variance of the log increments must not change with time.
candidates.methods: Exact simulation at the grid times: the exponential of a Brownian motion with drift.

candidates.name: Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process

competing.text: The process does not go back to a mean level.
The state takes only a few values.

tests: Autocorrelation: it must decrease exponentially with the time lag.
Stationary law: the values must have a normal marginal law.
candidates.methods: Exact simulation at the grid times: an AR(1) recursion with the exact transition law.

candidates.name: Poisson process

competing.text: Events make more events likely.

tests: Gaps between events: they must be independent and exponential.
Counts in disjoint windows must be independent.
candidates.methods: Add independent exponential gaps until the end of the window.

candidates.name: Compound Poisson process

competing.text: The process has infinitely many small jumps.

tests: Jump times: the gaps must be independent and exponential.
Jump sizes: they must be independent of the jump times.
candidates.methods: Draw the jump times as a Poisson process, then add independent jump sizes.

candidates.name: Branching process

competing.text: Events in continuous time trigger later events.

tests: Offspring law: check the counts of offspring of each parent.
Mean offspring: a mean above 1 gives growth with a positive probability. At most 1, the process ends with probability 1, unless each parent has exactly one offspring.
candidates.methods: Draw the offspring count of each member of each generation.

candidates.name: Hawkes process

competing.text: Events do not trigger other events.
The events form discrete generations.

tests: Time change: after the compensator transform, the gaps must be independent and exponential.
Branching ratio: the estimate must be below 1 for a stationary process.
candidates.methods: Ogata thinning, or the cluster method: immigrants as a Poisson process, then offspring of each event.

candidates.name: Lévy process

competing.text: There are only a few jumps in each period.
The path is continuous.

tests: Increments: they must be independent, with the same law for windows of the same length.
Small jumps: count the jumps above smaller and smaller thresholds.
candidates.methods: Exact increments when the page knows the law of an increment, or a compound Poisson approximation of the small jumps.

rules.reason: A yes-or-no result is a Bernoulli variable. Its law has one parameter: p = P(yes).
Each law on a finite list of labels is categorical. The parameters are the probabilities of the labels.
The counts of n independent draws, each with the same category probabilities, have the multinomial law.
Rank–frequency data often follow a power law. Zipf's law is a regularity of data, not a theorem.

rules.source: The standard law on the simplex
rules.reason: The Dirichlet law is the standard law for proportions with the sum 1. It is conjugate to the multinomial law. This is a common choice, not a theorem.
A vector of sums of many independent effects with finite variances, and no effect that dominates, is approximately multivariate normal.
The number of successes in n independent trials, each with probability p, has the Binomial(n, p) law.
The number of success items in n draws without replacement, from N items with K success items, has the Hypergeometric(N, K, n) law.

rules.source: Binomial limit of the hypergeometric law
rules.reason: When n is a small part of N, Binomial(n, K/N) is close to the hypergeometric law.

rules.source: Poisson process: independent increments and a constant rate
rules.reason: Independent events at a constant rate λ, in a window of size t, give a Poisson(λt) count. The counts in all windows form a Poisson process.
The number of failures before the first success, in independent trials with probability p, has the Geometric(p) law.

rules.source: Definition of the negative binomial law
rules.reason: The number of failures before success number r has the negative binomial law NB(r, p).

rules.source: Definitions of the geometric and negative binomial laws
rules.reason: The failures before the first success give a geometric law. The failures before success number r give a negative binomial law.
A Poisson count with a rate that has a gamma law between units is negative binomial.
A rate with a finite number of values gives a finite mixture of Poisson laws.
A rate that changes between units makes the variance larger than the mean. A Poisson law has a variance equal to its mean.

rules.source: Definition of the compound Poisson law
rules.reason: A total of N groups, with N ~ Poisson and independent group sizes with the same law, has a compound Poisson law.
A compound Poisson sum of group sizes with the logarithmic law is negative binomial.

rules.source: Definition of the discrete uniform law
rules.reason: Equal probabilities on the integers from a to b define the discrete uniform law.
These laws are common for counts. Without a mechanism, the rule graph cannot rank them.
A count with a fixed upper limit n needs a law on {0, …, n}. The binomial law is the simplest one with independent trials.
These laws give a positive probability to each count, also to counts above n.
These laws have a finite upper limit.
A Poisson law has a variance equal to its mean. This agreement supports the Poisson law, but it does not prove it.

rules.source: Moments of the negative binomial law
rules.reason: A negative binomial law has the variance μ + μ²/r, larger than its mean μ.
A compound Poisson count with group sizes above 1, a mixture of Poisson counts, and a geometric count all have a variance larger than the mean.

rules.source: Moments of the binomial and hypergeometric laws
rules.reason: A binomial variance np(1 − p) is smaller than the mean np. A hypergeometric variance is smaller still.
A Poisson law has a variance equal to its mean.

rules.source: Moments of the binomial and hypergeometric laws
rules.reason: These laws have a variance smaller than their mean.

rules.source: Moments of the negative binomial and geometric laws
rules.reason: These laws have a variance larger than their mean.
A Poisson law has a variance equal to its mean.
A count with extra zeros is a mixture of a point mass at 0 and another count law.
A Poisson law sets P(0) = e^(−λ) from its mean, so extra zeros do not fit it.
The exponential law is the only continuous law with no memory: P(T > s + t | T > s) = P(T > t).
The sum of k independent exponential stages with the same rate has the Erlang(k, λ) law.
A gamma law with a fitted shape is a common approximation when the stages have different rates.
The Weibull law has a hazard rate that is a power of the age. It is the most common law for wear and early failures.

rules.source: Other laws with a hazard rate that changes
rules.reason: These laws also have a hazard rate that changes with age.

rules.source: Constant hazard of the exponential law
rules.reason: Only the exponential law has a constant hazard rate. A hazard rate that changes with age excludes it.
A Weibull law with the shape k > 1 has the hazard rate (k/λ)(t/λ)^(k−1), which increases.
A gamma law with a shape above 1 has a hazard rate that increases to a constant.
The Gompertz law has the hazard rate b·e^(ct) with c > 0, which increases exponentially.
A Weibull hazard rate is a power of the age, not an exponential function.
A Weibull law with the shape k < 1 has a hazard rate that decreases.
A mix of strong and weak units, each with a constant hazard rate, has a hazard rate that decreases, because the weak units fail first. The hazard rate α/(σ + t) of the Pareto II law also decreases.

rules.source: Hazard rates that increase, then decrease
rules.reason: The log-logistic law with a shape above 1 and the lognormal law have a hazard rate that increases, then decreases.
The Weibull and Gompertz hazard rates are monotone.

rules.source: Central limit theorem for log T
rules.reason: When T is a product of many independent positive factors, log T is a sum. When the logarithms have a finite variance, T is approximately lognormal.

rules.source: First passage of Brownian motion with drift
rules.reason: The first time that a Brownian motion with a positive drift gets to a level above its start has the inverse Gaussian law.
Without drift, the first passage time of a Brownian motion to a level has the Lévy law. Its mean is infinite.
A first passage time of a Brownian motion is inverse Gaussian with a positive drift, and Lévy without drift.
These laws are common for times. Without a mechanism, the rule graph cannot rank them.

rules.source: Central limit theorem for log X
rules.reason: A product of many independent positive factors has a logarithm that is a sum. When the logarithms have a finite variance, the size is approximately lognormal.

rules.source: A common law for positive sums
rules.reason: The gamma law is a common law for a sum of positive parts. Independent gamma parts with the same scale have a gamma sum.

A sum of many independent parts with a finite variance, and no part that dominates, is approximately normal. A normal law also gives negative values, so use it only when the mean is many standard deviations above 0.

rules.source: Definition of the compound Poisson law
rules.reason: A total of a Poisson number of independent amounts with the same law has a compound Poisson law.
A power law above a minimum value is the Pareto I law. A power law that starts at 0 is the Pareto II law.

rules.source: Definition of the Pareto I law
rules.reason: The Pareto I law has the survival function (x_m/x)^α for x ≥ x_m.

rules.source: Definition of the Pareto II law
rules.reason: The Pareto II law has the survival function (1 + x/σ)^(−α) for x ≥ 0, with a density that decreases from its maximum at x = 0.

rules.source: Special cases of the Burr XII law
rules.reason: The Pareto II law is the case c = 1 of the Burr XII law.

rules.source: Body and tail shapes of the Burr XII law
rules.reason: When c > 1, the Burr XII law has a mode above 0 and a power-law tail, with separate shape parameters for the body and the tail.

rules.source: Special cases of the Burr XII law
rules.reason: The log-logistic law is the case k = 1 of the Burr XII law.
The excesses over a high threshold have approximately a generalised Pareto law, when the law is in the domain of attraction of an extreme-value law.
A normalised sum of many independent values with the same law, and a balanced regularly varying tail of index α < 2, converges to a stable law.
These laws are common for positive sizes. Without a mechanism, the rule graph cannot rank them.

rules.source: The standard law for a probability
rules.reason: The beta law is the standard law for an unknown probability. It is conjugate to the binomial law, so data change it in closed form.
With only the limits known, the uniform law is a common default. It has the largest entropy of all laws on the interval, but that is a choice, not knowledge.
These laws are common for proportions.
When the normalised maximum of a block has a limit law that is not a point mass, that limit is a generalised extreme value law.

rules.source: Limit laws of maxima and minima
rules.reason: The Weibull law is a limit law of minima. For maxima, its reflection, the reverse Weibull law, is the limit.
Values with a regularly varying tail of index α give maxima in the Fréchet domain, with the GEV shape ξ = 1/α > 0.
Values with an exponential, normal or lognormal type of tail give maxima in the Gumbel domain, with the GEV shape ξ = 0.
Values with a finite upper limit and a power law near that limit give maxima in the reverse Weibull domain, with ξ < 0.

rules.source: Limit law of minima: the weakest-link theorem
rules.reason: The minimum of many independent positive values, with a lower tail that behaves as a power near 0, is approximately Weibull.
The excesses over a high threshold have approximately a generalised Pareto law, when the law is in the domain of attraction of an extreme-value law.

rules.source: The two limit laws of extremes
rules.reason: Block maxima approximately follow a GEV law, and excesses over a threshold a generalised Pareto law.
A sum of many small independent effects, with finite variances and no effect that dominates, is approximately normal.

rules.source: Heavy tails of the t law
rules.reason: Student's t law has power-law tails, so large deviations are more frequent than for a normal law.
The Laplace and logistic laws have exponential tails, heavier than normal tails. The Cauchy law and the other stable laws with α < 2 have power-law tails with an infinite variance.
A normal law gives P(|X − μ| > 5σ) < 6·10^(−7). Frequent very large deviations do not fit it.
The difference of two independent exponential values with the same rate has the Laplace law.
The difference of two independent Gumbel values with the same scale has the logistic law.
The ratio of two independent normal values with mean 0 has the Cauchy law. Its mean does not exist.
A normalised sum of many independent values with the same law, and a balanced regularly varying tail of index α < 2, converges to a stable law.
A sum of squares of k independent standard normal values has the χ²(k) law.
A ratio of two independent chi-square values, each divided by its degrees of freedom, has the F law.
For normal data, the mean minus μ, divided by its estimated standard error, has Student's t law with n − 1 degrees of freedom.
Equal probability for all values between the limits defines the continuous uniform law. Make sure that all values between the limits have equal probability.

A continuous law gives the probability 0 to each exact value.

With many data, the empirical law keeps the atoms of the data.
A population of groups with different laws has the mixture law Σ w_i f_i.
For counts, a continuous mix of Poisson rates with a gamma law gives the negative binomial law.

The chance to record a value depends on the value. Then the recorded values do not have the law of the quantity. Without a model of the selection, the data cannot identify the law.
The interview does not know the observation mechanism. The model record assumes an exact record of each value.
The interview does not know if the values are independent. A marginal law does not define dependence. The model record assumes independent values.
Values close in time depend on each other. A law of one value does not define this dependence, so the model needs a process.
In continuous time, a stationary Gaussian Markov process that is continuous in probability and not constant is an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process.
A finite Markov chain that starts from its stationary law is a stationary process.
A process on a finite set of states, with a next state that depends only on the current state, is a finite Markov chain.
Brownian motion with drift has independent normal increments. Geometric Brownian motion has independent normal log increments, so it stays positive.
A positive quantity needs a process that stays positive. Geometric Brownian motion stays positive.
A quantity that can be negative, with changes that add, fits Brownian motion with drift.
An Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process goes back to its mean level, and it is stationary when it starts from its stationary law. A drift excludes it.

rules.source: Definition of the compound Poisson process
rules.reason: A process with jumps at the times of a Poisson process, and independent jump sizes, is a compound Poisson process.
Brownian motion has continuous paths, so jumps exclude it.
A process with stationary independent increments and infinitely many small jumps in each time interval is a Lévy process with an infinite jump intensity.
A point process in which each event raises the rate of later events is a Hawkes process.
A Hawkes process is a branching process of immigrants and their offspring. Its counts in windows have overdispersion, so a negative binomial count can approximate them.
Self-excitation makes the counts in windows overdispersed, so a Poisson count does not fit.
A population in which each member has an independent random number of offspring is a branching process.
The law of a generation size follows from the offspring law. In general it has no closed form, so simulate the process.
A conditional model states the law of one variable given the others. It suits a variable that depends on a cause.
A Gaussian copula keeps the marginal laws and adds a correlation matrix.
A joint law is its marginal laws and a copula. A marginal law does not define dependence, so choose the copula apart from the marginal laws.

rules.source: Tail dependence of the Gumbel copula
rules.reason: The Gumbel copula has the upper tail dependence 2 − 2^(1/θ), larger than 0 for θ > 1, and no lower tail dependence.
